analogy.p: Using GNI per capita alone to judge development is like judging a student by only their maths mark. It tells you something real, but it ignores English, science, attendance and effort. A fuller report card (birth rate, infant mortality, literacy, safe water) shows more, and the HDI is like a single overall grade that combines the main subjects. Even an overall grade can hide a student who is brilliant at one subject and struggling at another, just as a national average hides rich and poor. The analogy breaks down because a country is not a single student: it contains millions of people with very different experiences.

bullets: **Define** development and know why it is hard to measure with a single number.
**Economic measures**: GNI per capita (and GDP), plus employment structure (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary).
**Social measures**: birth rate, death rate, infant mortality rate, life expectancy, literacy rate and percentage with access to safe water.
**Composite measure**: the Human Development Index combines health, education and income into one value between 0 and 1.
Know the **limitations**: averages hide inequality, data can be unreliable, and single measures miss quality of life.
Know how to **link measures to the level of development**: an HIC typically has high GNI, long life expectancy and a tertiary-dominated workforce; an LIC the opposite.

Typical question types: define a term (1 mark), calculate or read a value (1-2 marks), describe a pattern in data (2-3 marks), explain a limitation (2-4 marks), evaluate which measure is best (6 marks).
Used again in the rest of the unit: the Demographic Transition Model, causes of uneven development, reducing the development gap and the Nigeria case study.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8035 Paper 2 (The changing economic world) begins with **measuring development**. You must be able to define development, classify countries by level of development, and use a range of **economic and social measures**: GNI per capita, birth rate, death rate, infant mortality, life expectancy, literacy rate, access to safe water, employment structure and the **Human Development Index (HDI)**. You must also explain the **limitations** of each type of measure and how the measures link to a country's stage of development. Questions are often data-based, so you need to calculate, compare and interpret figures as well as recall definitions.

bullets: **Economic development** = growth in wealth and the types of jobs, such as moving from farming to manufacturing and services.
**Social development** = improvements in health, education, housing, water and sanitation.
**Political development** = stable government, human rights, low corruption, and a say for citizens.
**Standard of living** is about wealth and material goods; **quality of life** is wider and includes wellbeing, safety and freedom, which are harder to measure.
Development is **relative**: people compare countries along a spectrum from least to most developed.
Development is a **process**, not a fixed state: countries can move up, and sometimes slip back after conflict, disease or economic shocks.
**Economic growth is not the same as development**: a country's income can rise while many people remain poor and unhealthy.
Indicator = a statistic used to measure some aspect of development; the spec expects you to know a range of them.
core.p: **Development** is the progress a country makes in improving the economic wealth and the quality of life of its people. It is not just about money: it includes better health, education, housing, safety, freedom and access to services. Because development covers many things, geographers use several indicators instead of one. Development is also a process, so countries move along it at different speeds, and a country can improve on some measures while stagnating on others.

bullets: **HICs**: high GNI per capita, high HDI, long life expectancy, low birth and infant mortality rates, most people employed in tertiary and quaternary jobs. Examples: UK, USA, Germany, Japan, Norway.

**NEEs**: moving from LIC to HIC, with rapid growth in manufacturing and urbanisation; rising incomes and improving health but with large inequality. Examples: China, India, Brazil, Mexico, Nigeria (the spec case study) and South Africa.

**LICs**: low GNI per capita, low HDI, high birth and death rates, high infant mortality, many people employed in primary jobs such as farming. Examples: Niger, Chad, Somalia, Malawi (check your teacher's list).
The World Bank classifies countries into income groups using GNI per capita thresholds, which are updated each year, so avoid memorising exact values.
**Newly industrialised countries** is another name you may meet; focus on the spec term NEE.
Classifications are **generalisations**: Brazil and Nigeria are both NEEs but have very different levels of income and HDI.
Countries can **move between categories** over time, for example South Korea moved from LIC to HIC within a few decades.
A single classification hides differences **within** a country, such as rich cities and poor rural regions.
core.h: Classifying countries: HICs, NEEs and LICs
core.p: Geographers group countries into three main categories using measures such as income and human development. **Higher income countries (HICs)** have high average incomes and well-developed services, **newly emerging economies (NEEs)** are experiencing rapid economic growth, typically driven by industrialisation, and **lower income countries (LICs)** have low incomes and widespread poverty. These are broad groups with fuzzy boundaries, and countries within a group can still differ greatly. The categories replace older, less precise labels such as 'First World' and 'Third World', and 'developed' and 'developing'.

bullets: **Formula**: GNI per capita = total GNI / population (for example US$420 billion / 35 million = US$12 000 per person).
**GDP** counts production within a country's borders; **GNI** adds income earned abroad by residents and subtracts income sent abroad by foreigners.
**Per capita** means 'per person': it lets small and large countries be compared fairly.
**Purchasing power parity (PPP)** adjusts incomes for local prices, so US$1 can buy more in a low-price country; HDI uses PPP-adjusted income.
**Strength**: simple, easily calculated and widely available for most countries.
**Limitation 1**: it is an **average**, so it hides inequality; a few very wealthy people can raise the mean while most remain poor.
**Limitation 2**: it ignores the **informal economy** (unregistered work, subsistence farming) which can be large in LICs and NEEs.
**Limitation 3**: it says nothing about **quality of life**, health, education, environment or freedom.
**Limitation 4**: exchange-rate changes and unreliable data (for example in countries with conflict or weak statistics offices) affect accuracy.
**Link**: HICs usually have high GNI per capita and LICs low, but oil-rich countries can have high GNI with low human development.
core.p: **Gross National Income (GNI)** is the total value of all goods and services produced by a country's residents and businesses in a year, including income earned from abroad. **GNI per capita** divides this by the population: **GNI per capita = total GNI / total population**. It is usually given in US dollars so that countries can be compared, and it is the standard economic measure of development in AQA questions. **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** is similar but measures value produced inside the country's borders. A higher GNI per capita generally means more money available for health, education and infrastructure.

bullets: **Birth rate** = (number of live births / total population) x 1000 per year; units are 'per 1000 per year'.
**Death rate** = (number of deaths / total population) x 1000 per year.
**Natural increase (per 1000)** = birth rate - death rate; divide by 10 to get a percentage.
**LICs**: very high birth rates (often over 30 per 1000) and relatively high death rates; **HICs**: low birth and death rates (often 8 to 12 per 1000).
**Why birth rates fall with development**: contraception and family planning, women's education and careers, lower infant mortality, urban living costs, and less need for child labour.
**Limitation**: death rate depends on **age structure** - an HIC with many elderly people can have a higher death rate than an LIC with a young population, despite better health care.
**Limitation**: they show population change more than quality of life; census data may be inaccurate where registration of births and deaths is incomplete.
**Link**: stages of the Demographic Transition Model map onto stages of development, so these measures help place a country on the DTM.
core.p: The **birth rate** is the number of live births per 1000 people in a year, and the **death rate** is the number of deaths per 1000 people in a year. The difference between them is the **natural change** (natural increase if births exceed deaths). In LICs the birth rate tends to be high because of limited contraception, high infant mortality, the need for children to work or provide security, and lower education for women. As health care, education and incomes improve, death rates fall first and birth rates fall later. This pattern forms the basis of the Demographic Transition Model.

bullets: **Infant mortality rate** = (infant deaths under 1 year / live births) x 1000; units: per 1000 live births.
**Life expectancy** is an **average at birth**; high infant mortality drags the average down, so LICs often have life expectancy of 55 to 65 and HICs of 80 or more.
**Causes of low life expectancy in LICs**: disease (malaria, HIV/AIDS), poor sanitation, malnutrition, conflict and limited medical care.
**Causes of high life expectancy in HICs**: advanced medicine, good nutrition, clean water, safe work and welfare systems.
**Gender gap**: women typically live longer than men in most countries; some data are given separately.
**Strength**: they are good indicators of overall health and wellbeing and are usually reliably recorded.
**Limitation**: they are **averages** and conceal differences between rich and poor, urban and rural, and ethnic groups.
**Limitation**: they measure health only; they do not show income, education or political freedom.
**Link**: improved infant mortality is a main driver of falling birth rates and rising life expectancy as countries develop.
core.p: The **infant mortality rate** is the number of babies who die before their first birthday per 1000 live births per year. **Life expectancy** is the average number of years a person is expected to live from birth. Both are strong indicators of health care, nutrition, sanitation and income. In LICs, infant mortality is high because of poor sanitation, disease, malnutrition and limited access to doctors and vaccinations, so life expectancy is lower. HICs have the opposite pattern, with strong health systems and healthy lifestyles.

bullets: **Literacy rate** = (number of literate adults / adult population) x 100%.
**Why literacy matters**: educated people get better jobs, earn more, have healthier families and have fewer children.
**Why safe water matters**: contaminated water spreads cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea, which cause many child deaths; collecting water takes time that could be spent on school or work.
**LICs**: low literacy (sometimes under 50%) and limited access to safe water; **HICs**: close to 100% for both.
**Strength**: easy to understand and directly linked to quality of life.
**Limitation**: literacy definitions vary between countries ('can read and write a simple sentence') and say little about education quality.
**Limitation**: 'access' may mean a standpipe 1 km away rather than water in the home, and supply may be unreliable or unsafe.
**Limitation**: national averages hide gender gaps and urban versus rural differences.
**Link**: both are part of the standard measures used to judge progress toward development goals.
core.h: Literacy rate and access to safe water
core.p: The **literacy rate** is the percentage of adults (usually aged 15 and over) who can read and write. **Access to safe water** is the percentage of the population with a clean, protected supply of drinking water. Both are social measures that show whether basic needs are being met. Education raises skills, productivity and incomes, while safe water reduces disease, especially among children. In many LICs women and rural people have lower literacy and poorer access to safe water than men and urban populations.

bullets: **LICs**: most people in the primary sector (often over 50%), often subsistence farming, with small secondary and tertiary sectors.
**NEEs**: the secondary sector grows rapidly as factories open, with rising numbers in the tertiary sector as incomes grow; the primary share falls.
**HICs**: most people in the tertiary sector (often 70 to 80% or more), a small primary share (under about 5%) and a significant quaternary sector.
**Why the shift happens**: mechanisation reduces farm labour, foreign investment brings industry, rising incomes increase demand for services and education creates skilled workers.
**Strength**: shows the stage of economic development, and gives clues about wages and skills.
**Limitation**: it does not show income or standard of living; some primary jobs, such as mining, may be well paid, and tertiary jobs can be low paid.
**Limitation**: the **informal sector** is often missing from the data in LICs and NEEs.
**Limitation**: national averages hide regional differences, such as industrial cities and farming regions.
**Link**: employment structure ties into the Clark-Fisher model of change and into the later study of deindustrialisation in the UK.
core.p: **Employment structure** shows the proportion of a country's workers in each of the sectors of the economy: **primary** (extracting raw materials such as farming, fishing, mining), **secondary** (manufacturing and construction), **tertiary** (services such as teaching, retail and healthcare) and **quaternary** (high-tech research and information-based work). As a country develops, the main employment shifts from primary to secondary and then to tertiary and quaternary jobs. Therefore, the percentage of workers in each sector is a useful indicator of development. It is a measure of economic structure rather than directly of living standards.

bullets: **Three components**: health (life expectancy), education (mean and expected years of schooling) and income (GNI per capita, PPP).
**Scale**: 0 (lowest) to 1 (highest); UNDP bands: **very high** about 0.800 and above, **high** about 0.700 to 0.799, **medium** about 0.550 to 0.699, **low** below about 0.550.
**Typical results**: countries such as Norway, Switzerland and Iceland score very high; countries such as Niger, Chad and South Sudan are among the lowest.
**Strengths**: combines economic and social measures, is simple, is published for most countries and is comparable over time.
**Limitation 1**: it is still an **average**, hiding inequality and differences between regions, men and women, and ethnic groups.
**Limitation 2**: it leaves out important factors such as **environmental sustainability, political freedom, human rights, safety and inequality** (though UNDP publishes adjusted versions).
**Limitation 3**: it gives equal weighting to all three components, which can be debated, and some data may be estimated.
**Limitation 4**: a single score cannot capture individual experiences or subjective wellbeing.
**Exam tip**: when asked why HDI is better than GNI per capita, say it includes health and education, not just income.
core.p: The **Human Development Index (HDI)** is a **composite index** published by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). It combines three dimensions of human development into a single number between 0 and 1: a **long and healthy life** (life expectancy at birth), **knowledge** (years of schooling) and a **decent standard of living** (GNI per capita, adjusted for purchasing power). A value closer to 1 means higher human development. HDI is useful because it blends social and economic factors rather than relying on one measure, and it lets countries be ranked and compared.

bullets: **Averages hide inequality**: a high GNI per capita can coexist with extreme poverty if wealth is concentrated; the **median** or the Gini coefficient would be more informative.
**Hidden economies**: informal work, subsistence farming and unrecorded trade are missing from GNI.
**Data quality**: conflict, weak statistics offices, political manipulation and infrequent censuses make some figures unreliable or out of date.
**Single indicators are narrow**: GNI ignores health and education; life expectancy ignores income; literacy ignores quality of schooling.
**Quality of life is subjective**: happiness, safety, freedom, culture and environment are hard to measure.
**Context**: a resource-rich country can have high GNI because of oil but poor health and education, so figures may mislead without other indicators.
**Cost of living differs**: US$1 buys more in some countries than others unless adjusted by PPP.
**Time lags**: development changes quickly, but datasets can be a few years old by publication.
**Uneven across a country**: urban and rural, men and women, rich and poor regions.
core.h: Limitations of economic and social measures
core.p: The spec specifically requires you to know the limitations of both economic and social indicators. Every measure only tells part of the story, and most are averages that hide how resources are shared. The reliability of data also varies, so no single indicator should be used alone. Examiners reward answers that explain **why** a limitation matters, not just name it. Combining several indicators (or using HDI) gives a more reliable picture of development.

bullets: **LIC profile**: low GNI, high birth, death and infant mortality rates, short life expectancy, low literacy, limited safe water, mainly primary jobs, low HDI.
**NEE profile**: rapidly rising GNI, falling birth and infant mortality rates, growing secondary and tertiary employment, medium to high HDI, large inequality.
**HIC profile**: high GNI, low birth and death rates, very low infant mortality, long life expectancy, near-universal literacy and safe water, tertiary-dominated jobs, very high HDI.
**Cause and effect**: better health care and education improve productivity, which raises GNI, which allows more investment in health and education (a positive feedback loop).
**DTM link**: LICs are typically in stages 1 to 2, NEEs in stage 3, HICs in stage 4 or 5 of the demographic transition model.
**Exceptions**: oil-rich states (high GNI, lower HDI) and countries with high health but low income (some small island states) show that measures do not always move together.
**Use several indicators** to place a country, because the combination gives a more reliable picture than any single measure.
**Data tip**: compare pairs of countries, quote both values and say 'X is higher than Y by...'.
core.h: Linking measures to stages of development
core.p: Countries at different stages of development show recognisable patterns across the indicators. As development progresses, GNI per capita, life expectancy, literacy and HDI rise, while birth rate, death rate and infant mortality fall, and the employment structure shifts toward tertiary and quaternary jobs. Most relationships are strong but not perfect: for example, life expectancy rises steeply with income at low levels, then flattens at high income. NEEs often show rapid change in several measures at once but with big inequalities. Linking measures in this way lets you describe a country's stage of development with evidence.

bullets: **Describe first**: 'As GNI per capita increases, life expectancy increases' (and give a range with units, such as 'from 52 to 82 years').
**Use anomalies**: point out a country that does not fit the trend and suggest why (for example oil wealth, conflict or health policy).
**Quote data**: use figures from the source, with units, and calculate differences or ratios when asked.
**Choropleth maps**: read the key carefully, describe the global distribution, and refer to continents or regions.
**Correlation is not causation**: higher income is linked with, but is not the sole cause of, longer life expectancy.
**Calculation skills**: mean, median, range, percentage change, and natural change (birth rate - death rate).
**Percentage change** = (new - old) / old x 100.
**Be careful with 'per 1000' units**: infant mortality of 34 per 1000 means 3.4%, not 34%.
**Check the axis scale** and whether units are in thousands or millions.
core.h: Interpreting data and graphs on development
core.p: Many exam questions give a table of development indicators or a graph (a scatter graph, bar chart or choropleth map) and ask you to describe patterns or use the data. A high-scoring answer states the trend, quotes figures with units, makes a comparison and then offers a reason. Scatter graphs, such as life expectancy against GNI per capita, usually show a **positive correlation** that flattens at high incomes. A **choropleth map** shades countries by value, and you should describe the global pattern (for example, high HDI in Europe and North America, low HDI in much of sub-Saharan Africa) with at least two named areas.

bullets: **Causes of uneven development**: physical (climate, resources, hazards), economic (trade, debt) and historical (colonialism, conflict) factors explain why indicators differ.
**Reducing the development gap**: aid, debt relief, fair trade, microfinance, investment and industrial development aim to raise the indicators.
**Nigeria case study**: use GNI, HDI, employment structure and life expectancy to show where it stands as an NEE, and note the differences between regions.
**UK economy**: the shift from secondary to tertiary and quaternary employment shows an HIC's structure changing.
**Global inequality**: gaps between the highest and lowest HDI countries remain large, driving migration and international debate.
**Urbanisation**: as countries develop, people move from rural to urban areas, changing employment and birth rates.
**Sustainable development**: development should meet current needs without compromising future generations, so environmental indicators are increasingly considered.
**Fieldwork and Paper 3 skills**: choosing and justifying the best indicator is the same skill as evaluating enquiry data.
core.h: Links to other topics and wider case study use
core.p: Measuring development is the base for the rest of the Changing economic world topic, and the skills reappear throughout the course. The indicators let you identify the **causes of uneven development**, evaluate strategies that **reduce the development gap**, and judge how far a country such as Nigeria has developed. They also connect with population and urban topics, such as the DTM and rapid urbanisation in LICs and NEEs. Refer to specific indicators in extended writing to add precision and evidence.

exam: **Command words**: 'Define' (give meaning), 'Calculate' (show working and units), 'Describe' (say what the data shows with figures), 'Explain' (reason with 'because'), 'Evaluate' (weigh up and conclude).
**1 mark definitions**: use exact phrases, such as 'GNI per capita is the average income per person' or 'infant mortality is deaths of babies under 1 per 1000 live births'.
**Calculations**: write the formula, substitute, then state the answer with units, for example GNI per capita = total GNI / population.
**Describe patterns in data**: state the overall trend, quote at least two figures with units, and mention any anomaly.
**Limitation answers (2-4 marks)**: name the limitation, then explain it with 'because' or 'so' - for example 'GNI per capita is an average so it hides inequality'.

**6 mark evaluation ('which is the best measure?')**: discuss at least two measures, give strengths and limitations of each, and end with a justified conclusion (for example, HDI is better as it combines three factors, but it still hides inequality).
**Link indicators to stages**: always connect measures to LIC/NEE/HIC patterns with evidence.
**Use country names** and data if given; with maps, mention continents or regions.
**Units matter**: per 1000, per year, US$, years, %.
**Do not say** 'developed' or 'third world'; use HIC, NEE and LIC.
**Choose your words**: 'average', 'inequality', 'informal economy', 'composite index', 'quality of life' score marks.

mistakes.r: Development includes economic wealth and quality of life: health, education, safe water, freedom and more.
It is the average income per person (total GNI divided by population) and does not show how income is shared.
mistakes.w: 'GNI per capita is the total wealth of a country.'

mistakes.r: GNI per capita is an average; inequality means many people may still be poor.
mistakes.w: 'A high GNI means everyone is well off.'

mistakes.r: It is the number of babies who die before age 1 per 1000 live births.
mistakes.w: 'Infant mortality is the number of children who die.'

mistakes.r: HDI combines life expectancy, education (schooling) and income, so it measures both social and economic development.
It is an average expected length of life from birth, so it is affected by infant deaths.
mistakes.w: 'Life expectancy is how long people will actually live.'

mistakes.r: It is births per 1000 people per year; always give the 'per 1000' unit.
mistakes.w: 'Birth rate is the number of babies born.'

mistakes.r: Employment structure shows the type of work, not wages; the shift from primary to tertiary is a typical sign of development.
mistakes.w: 'Primary jobs are bad and tertiary jobs are good.'

mistakes.r: Explain: 'averages hide inequality because rich people raise the mean, so many people could be poorer than the figure suggests'.
mistakes.w: 'The limitation is that it isn't accurate.' (vague)

summary: The specification asks you to know how development is defined and measured: HIC, NEE and LIC classification, GNI per capita, birth and death rates, infant mortality, life expectancy, literacy, safe water, employment structure and the Human Development Index, plus the limitations of each and how they link to stages of development. It matters because every later topic in the Changing economic world unit, and many data questions, depend on using these indicators accurately.

terms.d: The progress a country makes in improving the economic wealth and quality of life of its people.
A country with a high average income and well-developed economy, services and quality of life.
A country experiencing rapid economic growth, usually driven by industrialisation, and moving from low to high income.
A country with a low average income, widespread poverty and a lower level of development.
The total value of goods and services produced by a country's residents in a year, including income from abroad.
The total GNI of a country divided by its population; the average income per person, usually in US dollars.
The total value of goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year.
The number of live births per 1000 people in a population per year.
The number of deaths per 1000 people in a population per year.
The number of babies per 1000 live births who die before reaching their first birthday.
The average number of years a person can expect to live, measured from birth.
The percentage of adults who can read and write.
The proportion of a country's workforce employed in each of the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary sectors.
A composite measure from 0 to 1 combining life expectancy, education and income per person, used to rank countries by human development.
A statistic used to measure a particular aspect of development.
An adjustment for differences in the cost of living so that incomes can be compared in terms of what they can actually buy.
The difference between the birth rate and the death rate; positive when births exceed deaths.

worked.ans: GNI per capita = US$12 000 per person (1 mark for method, 1 for answer with units).
worked.q: Country A has a total GNI of US$420 billion and a population of 35 million. Calculate its GNI per capita. Show your working. (2 marks)
steps: Formula: GNI per capita = total GNI / population.
Convert to the same units: US$420 billion = 420 000 000 000; 35 million = 35 000 000.

worked.q: In Country B, infant mortality fell from 62 per 1000 live births in 2000 to 34 per 1000 in 2020. Literacy rose from 62% to 79%. (a) Calculate the percentage fall in infant mortality. (b) By how many percentage points did literacy rise? (c) Give one reason why infant mortality may have fallen. (4 marks)
steps: (c) Link to causes: better health care, vaccination, clean water or nutrition.

worked.ans: GNI per capita is useful because it is simple, widely available and allows countries to be compared using one number, and income gives people the means to pay for health, food and education (2). However, it is an average, so it hides inequality: a country with a few billionaires can have a high figure although many people remain poor (1). It also ignores the informal economy, such as subsistence farming, and says nothing about health, education or freedom, so an oil-rich country may have high GNI per capita but low life expectancy and literacy (1). The Human Development Index is more reliable because it combines income with life expectancy and years of schooling (1). I therefore only partly agree: GNI per capita is a helpful starting point, but a combination of GNI with social indicators or the HDI gives a more complete picture of development, although even these are averages and miss differences within countries (1).
worked.q: 'GNI per capita is the best measure of how developed a country is.' To what extent do you agree? (6 marks)
steps: State what GNI per capita measures and its strengths.
Give limitations: average, informal economy, ignores quality of life.
Compare with HDI or social indicators such as life expectancy and literacy.
